summary: Grade 4 measurement line plots at eighth-inch precision, fused with using the plotted data for fraction arithmetic. Learners measure specimens to the nearest 1/8 inch, build an equal-interval eighth scale, plot one X per object, then answer genuine questions that require adding and subtracting fractions with like/related denominators: the difference between longest and shortest, and the total length of everything. The key insight comes when totalling over stacks: three Xs at 3/8 contribute 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8, so frequency (how many Xs) and value (how much length) diverge. Marking 2/8 = 1/4 and 4/8 = 1/2 on the axis makes common denominators visible, so 1/2 − 3/8 becomes 4/8 − 3/8 right on the scale.
misconceptions: When asked for a total length, adding or counting the Xs (frequency) instead of summing the measured values
Adding fractions by adding numerators AND denominators (3/8 + 3/8 = 6/16)
Spacing eighths unequally or not seeing 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½, so scales don't line up and common denominators are missed
Counting a value only once when several Xs are stacked on it while totalling

activities.title: Build-then-compute an eighth-inch line plot
steps: Measure several real objects (e.g. seedlings or paper strips) to the nearest 1/8 inch using a ruler subdivided into eighths; include some objects that share a length.
Draw a number line marked in equally spaced intervals that each represent 1/8 inch, and plot one X per object at its measured value.
Mark where 2/8 lines up with 1/4 and where 4/8 lines up with 1/2 directly on the axis.
Find longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions, converting to a common denominator on the scale (e.g. 1/2 − 3/8 = 4/8 − 3/8 = 1/8).
Find the total length of all objects by adding each object's value with multiplicity — a stack of three Xs at 3/8 contributes 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8, not '3'.
Predict how the total changes if one more object at 1/2 is added, then check (the total rises by 1/2 = 4/8).
activities.insight: An accurate eighth scale makes equivalences (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2) and common denominators visible, and totalling over a plot means summing measured values with multiplicity — which is different from counting Xs.

activities.title: Compute from a given plot: difference and total
steps: From a pre-drawn eighth-scale plot, state the longest and shortest values and compute longest − shortest over a common denominator.
Compute the total length, taking care that a stack of several Xs at one value contributes that value once per X.
Choose which of several candidate totals is correct, and explain why the count of Xs is NOT the total length.
activities.insight: Given an accurate plot, the difference and total are determined by reading positions and adding/subtracting fractions correctly, keeping multiplicity in mind.

activities.title: Reveal equivalence on the eighth scale (reference scaffold)
steps: Tap or point to a position on an eighth-scale line and read off its equivalent (2/8 = 1/4, 4/8 = 1/2).
Tap a stack of Xs to reveal its combined contribution to the total (e.g. three Xs at 3/8 reveal 3/8 + 3/8 + 3/8 = 9/8).
Name where 1/4 and 1/2 sit and what else each is the same as.
activities.insight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same point on an eighth scale, and a stack's contribution is its value repeated once per X.

checkQuestion: Give the child a ruler marked in eighths and several objects, some sharing a length. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest eighth inch, plot them, then tell me the difference between the longest and shortest, and the total length of all of them.' Watch the scale-building, and especially watch how they handle stacks of more than one X when totalling, and how they subtract the two fractional positions.
checkAnswer: Builds an equal-interval eighth-inch scale, plots one X per object, finds longest − shortest by subtracting the two fractional positions over a common denominator, and totals by adding each object's value WITH multiplicity (a stack of three at 3/8 contributes 3/8 three times), recognising 2/8 = ¼ and 4/8 = ½.
